title: The 10 Best Outlet Testers
subtitle: Plug-in GFCI and receptacle testers for checking outlet wiring, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: An outlet tester plugs into a receptacle and shows in seconds whether it's wired correctly and whether a GFCI trips. We ranked 10 best-sellers from Klein Tools, Fluke, Southwire, Sperry, Ideal and value brands on rating, review volume and features (a GFCI test, a voltage readout, open-fault detection, a safety listing and extra functions).
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

avoid.name: Sahanula Outlet Tester with GFCI Check, Grounding and Receptacle Circuit Tester (SA051)
avoid.flag: No listing for safety standards; model field is a database ID
avoid.verdict: A plug-in tester whose listing never says which wiring faults it detects or what standard it meets, for a tool you trust to tell you a circuit is safe.
reasons: The bullets promise it 'accurately' checks wiring but never list the faults it detects, the GFCI trip current, or any UL or CSA listing.
The model number field is a random database string (a UUID), not a model number, and the bullets misspell the brand as 'shahanula'.
For the same price, Klein's RT110 is UL 1436 and CSA certified with 3,599 reviews.

buyers_guide.q: What does an outlet tester show?
buyers_guide.a: Plug it in and the lights or screen show whether the outlet is wired correctly or has an open ground, open neutral, open hot, or reversed hot and neutral.

buyers_guide.q: Do I need a GFCI test button?
buyers_guide.a: Yes for kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoors. The button leaks a small current to ground so you can confirm the GFCI actually trips.
Basic testers can miss a hot-ground reverse combined with an open ground, and they can't judge connection quality. They're a quick check, not a full inspection.
Light codes are cheap and fine for a yes/no. An LCD shows actual voltage, which helps spot low-voltage problems and makes faults easier to read.
Newer homes use arc-fault breakers in bedrooms and living areas. Only testers like the Klein RT310 can simulate an arc fault to check them.
